newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya government urges investors to stay calm.
newsitem.headline: Kenya government urges investors to stay calm.

text.p: Kenya's government urged investors to stay calm and citizens to build the economy in an attempt to ease pressure caused by a weakening shilling and an air traffic dispute.
"The cabinet wishes to assure Kenyans and investors in general that the situation is under control," said a statement broadcast on state television and radio late on Monday.

"Kenyans are urged to continue building the economy based on their own resources so that the development of the country remains firmly in their hands," said the statement whose reception was disrupted by a power cut. The statement contained no specific proposals.

Kenya's President Daniel arap Moi, 73 and in power for 19 years and the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) are widely expected to win elections that must be held by the end of this year. They face an opposition that has found a fragile cohesion in demands for constitutional reforms.

In an apparent appeal to bilateral donors not to follow the lead set by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the government said it welcomed support from development partners. The IMF last Thursday suspended a $205 million three-year loan citing concerns over corruption.
The government on Monday proposed air traffic controllers end a go-slow over pay and return to work, an airport manager said.
The strike at Kenya's main airports has delayed traffic for up to 12 hours and caused cancellations at one of the year's busiest periods for one of Africa's main tourist destinations.

The government said the controllers, who started a go-slow at midnight on Friday and have been joined by meteorologists, give it two weeks to consider pay commitments made to end a previous go-slow last December, the manager said.
"The go-slow is in its third day and it is absolute chaos out there," said an air traffic controller at Kenyatta Airport.
The Kenyan shilling's international value slid on Monday with high dollar demand, weakening to close at 63, 3.25 percent down from Monday's opening, according to commercial bank rates.
Attorney-General Amos Wako unveiled on Monday plans to review the constitution. But his protracted timetable fell far short of opposition demands.
Wako published a draft bill on Monday to create a commission to review the constitution and said it had up to three years to report to Moi.
An opposition-backed reform group has called a general strike for Friday.
